C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 22-year-old woman has a firm, bulbous nodule at the site of an ear piercing performed two years ago. The lesion extends well beyond the original piercing site and has continued to enlarge. What distinguishes this from a hypertrophic scar?
opts: It stays within the wound margins
Staying within the wound margins is the hypertrophic scar pattern. Extension beyond them is the defining keloid feature.
It extends beyond the margins and does not regress

Correct. A keloid extends beyond the wound site margins, develops slowly, continues to enlarge for months to years, and shows no regression with a tendency to recur. A hypertrophic scar develops rapidly within four weeks, remains within the wound margins, and flattens with time.
It developed within four weeks
Rapid development within four weeks characterises a hypertrophic scar. The keloid develops slowly and keeps enlarging over months to years.
It is always painless
Keloids are often asymptomatic but may be pruritic or produce burning pain, and hypertrophic scars are also typically asymptomatic. Symptoms do not separate them.
It flattens with time
Hypertrophic scars remain stable and regress with time. Keloids show no regression.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 13

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 28-year-old man presents with an abrupt eruption of small pustules on the thighs and buttocks. Each pustule sits on an erythematous base and is pierced by a central hair. He is afebrile with no systemic symptoms. He has type 2 diabetes and wears occlusive workout clothing. What is the most likely causative organism?
opts: Pseudomonas aeruginosa

Pseudomonas aeruginosa causes folliculitis occasionally, classically after exposure to inadequately chlorinated whirlpools, hot tubs, or water slides. No such exposure is described, and Staphylococcus aureus remains the commonest cause overall.
Streptococcus pyogenes
Streptococcus pyogenes is the most common organism in erysipelas and a cause of impetigo and cellulitis. It is not the characteristic organism of follicular pustules.
Candida albicans
Candida albicans is the most common pathogen in chronic paronychia and causes cutaneous candidiasis in moist occluded sites. A pustule pierced by a central hair is a bacterial follicular lesion.
Corynebacterium minutissimum
Corynebacterium minutissimum causes erythrasma, a chronic superficial infection of intertriginous skin that fluoresces coral-red under a Wood's lamp. It does not produce follicular pustules.
Staphylococcus aureus

Correct. Bacterial folliculitis is most commonly caused by Staphylococcus aureus. His diabetes and occlusive clothing are both listed risk factors, alongside obesity, poor hygiene, heat and humidity, immunocompromise, corticosteroids, and nasal carriage.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 39

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
C.q: A 58-year-old Black woman has had a pigmented band in the great toenail for two years that was previously attributed to trauma. Where does the tumour usually arise, and why is recognition delayed?
opts: In the nail bed; only fair-skinned patients
Assuming it is a sun-driven disease of fair skin is exactly the reasoning that produces delay in darker-skinned patients, and the matrix rather than the bed is the usual origin.
In the matrix; pain is always present
Pain and cold sensitivity characterise glomus tumour. Nail unit melanoma commonly presents as painless pigment change.
In the periungual skin; easily seen
Matrix tumours cause longitudinal plate changes, and the origin beneath the proximal fold is part of why they are recognised late.
In the matrix; it is rare and not sun-driven

Correct. Nail unit melanoma is a rare acral melanoma arising most often in the matrix. It is not clearly ultraviolet driven and may occur in any skin tone, and delayed recognition contributes to worse outcomes.
In the matrix; it is over-diagnosed
It is rare, and rarity combined with an unexpected demographic is what drives delay.
C.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 79

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 21-year-old woman presents with painful genital ulcers. The clinician considers alternative causes. Which differential is characteristically painless?
opts: Chancroid
Chancroid is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection caused by Haemophilus ducreyi producing painful necrotizing ulcers with inguinal lymphadenopathy. It is painful rather than painless.
Candidiasis
Candidiasis is on the differential and produces burning and pruritus with well-demarcated erythema and satellite lesions rather than a painless eroded papule.
Syphilis
Correct. Syphilis lesions start as solitary raised papules that erode and are usually painless, which is what distinguishes them from the painful ulcers of herpes simplex virus and chancroid.
Trauma
Trauma appears on the differential and is characteristically painful, so it does not provide the contrast the question asks for.
Herpes simplex recurrence
Herpes simplex virus produces grouped vesicles that break down into shallow painful ulcers, with localised pain and prodromal burning.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 121

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
C.q: A 26-year-old woman with vitiligo affecting more than 5 percent of her body surface area is being counselled on treatment. What is first-line, and why is one phototherapy option preferred over another?
opts: Topical therapy alone at any extent
Topical therapy is used when there is limited surface involvement below 5 percent. Relying on it for extensive disease under-treats the patient.
Psoralen with ultraviolet A preferred
This inverts the safety comparison. Psoralen with ultraviolet A is the option associated with increased skin cancer risk, which is why narrow band ultraviolet B is preferred.
Phototherapy, narrow band ultraviolet B preferred

Correct. Phototherapy is first line in patients with more than 5 percent body surface area involvement, and narrow band ultraviolet B is preferred over psoralen with ultraviolet A, which carries adverse effects including increased skin cancer risk. Combination of topical therapy with phototherapy is ideal.
No treatment is available
Effective options exist across the range of disease extent, and withholding them would leave a treatable condition untreated.
Surgical grafting for all patients
Management is multifactorial and depends on the extent of disease, with topical therapy and phototherapy preceding surgical approaches.
C.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 25

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 31-year-old man with progressive frontotemporal recession and early vertex thinning asks about treatment. He and his partner are not planning a pregnancy and he has no contraindications. Which statement about the two principal medical therapies is correct?
opts: Finasteride's sexual effects are permanent

About 2 percent of men taking finasteride report decreased libido and erectile function, but these effects are reversible when the drug is stopped. Telling a patient they are permanent would wrongly deter effective treatment.
Neither agent alters the course
Both agents prevent further hair loss and may produce some regrowth. Withholding effective therapy from a patient who has asked for it is not supported by the evidence presented in the lecture.
Finasteride is topical and minoxidil oral
The routes are reversed. Minoxidil is the topically applied agent and finasteride is the oral one, so a patient given this advice would apply and swallow the wrong drugs.
Finasteride is oral and works best with minoxidil

Correct. Finasteride prevents further hair loss and may provide some regrowth, and works best in combination with minoxidil. Dihydrotestosterone is the androgen chiefly responsible for the follicular miniaturisation, which is what the enzyme inhibition addresses.
Minoxidil works best at the frontal hairline
The region is wrong. Minoxidil prevents further loss and may lead to regrowth but is primarily effective in the crown region of the scalp, which is the opposite of what this states.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 148

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 52-year-old woman has a rapidly expanding painful ulcer with undermined violaceous borders, and repeated wound cultures are negative. What is the most accurate description of how pyoderma gangrenosum is diagnosed?
opts: Confirmed by wound culture
Cultures are negative in pyoderma gangrenosum, and that negativity is used to exclude infectious ulcers. Growth of an organism would point away from the diagnosis.
Confirmed by a specific biopsy finding

Biopsy supports the diagnosis and helps exclude alternatives, but there is no pathognomonic histological finding that confirms it. Treating a biopsy as confirmatory risks anchoring on the wrong diagnosis.
Confirmed by inflammatory bowel disease
Inflammatory bowel disease is a key associated condition, and it raises suspicion substantially, but the association is not diagnostic on its own.
A diagnosis of exclusion

Correct. Pyoderma gangrenosum is explicitly a diagnosis of exclusion. Infectious ulcers, which are culture negative in pyoderma gangrenosum, and vascular insufficiency ulcers assessed by ankle-brachial index must be ruled out.
Confirmed by a pathergy test
Pathergy is a clinical feature — worsening with trauma or debridement — rather than a validated confirmatory test performed on every patient.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 59

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 6-year-old unvaccinated child has a generalised pruritic eruption concentrated on the trunk, scalp, and face. Macules, papules, vesicles, and crusts are all present at the same time. What feature is most characteristic?
opts: Lesions limited to the palms and soles
Varicella lesions concentrate on the trunk, scalp, and face. Palm and sole involvement points elsewhere.
Lesions with honey-coloured crusting around the nose and mouth
Honey-coloured perioral crusting is impetigo, a superficial bacterial infection.
Lesions in multiple stages of healing appearing simultaneously

Correct. Primary varicella-zoster virus infection causes a generalised pruritic eruption in multiple stages of healing — macules progress to papules, vesicles, and crusts, with several stages appearing simultaneously.
Lesions confined to a single dermatome
Dermatomal confinement that abruptly stops at the midline describes herpes zoster, the reactivation of latent virus, rather than primary varicella.
Lesions all at the same stage of evolution
Uniform staging is what distinguishes other vesicular eruptions from varicella. Simultaneous multiple stages is the defining feature here.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 84

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 24-year-old man is diagnosed with pityriasis rosea. The eruption began four days ago and is mildly itchy. He is otherwise well and not pregnant-exposed or immunocompromised. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Oral terbinafine
Terbinafine treats dermatophyte infection. Tinea corporis is the classic mimic of the herald patch, but the diagnosis here is already established and pityriasis rosea is not a fungal disease.
Oral acyclovir for all patients
Acyclovir is reserved for severe cases, consistent with the suspected viral aetiology. Routine antiviral therapy for a mild self-limited eruption is not indicated.
Reassurance alone, no treatment for itch

Reassurance is the correct foundation but this stops one step short. The itch is treatable, and declining to address a symptom the patient has reported leaves him uncomfortable for the several weeks the eruption lasts.
Reassurance, with an antihistamine for itch

Correct. Pityriasis rosea is self-limited and the mainstay is reassurance. Oral antihistamines or topical steroids can be used cautiously for pruritus, and phototherapy or natural sunlight may help if begun in the first week of the eruption.
Oral prednisone over two weeks

A systemic corticosteroid is disproportionate for a self-limited eruption and carries a real hazard in anyone with a psoriatic tendency, since pustular psoriasis may follow systemic steroid withdrawal.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 171

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
C.q: A 68-year-old woman is told she has multiple actinic keratoses and asks whether that means she has skin cancer. What is the relationship between actinic keratosis and keratinocyte carcinoma?
opts: It progresses to basal cell carcinoma
The continuum is with keratinocyte carcinoma of squamous type. Basal cell carcinoma arises through a different route driven by intense intermittent exposure.
Entirely benign and unrelated
Treating it as benign discards the reason it is identified and treated at all, and the continuum with squamous cell carcinoma is what makes it worth eradicating.
Invasive carcinoma from the outset
It is a dysplastic change rather than invasive disease. Features suggesting invasion — thickness, induration, ulceration, bleeding — are what prompt biopsy.
It progresses to melanoma
Actinic keratosis is a keratinocytic lesion. Melanoma arises from melanocytes.
Premalignant, on a continuum with carcinoma

Correct. Chronic ultraviolet injury produces dysplastic keratinocytic change in a field of sun-damaged skin. Actinic keratosis is premalignant and lies on a biologic continuum with keratinocyte carcinoma.
C.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 11

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 36-year-old man has had hidradenitis suppurativa of both axillae for eight years despite antibiotics and repeated drainage, and asks whether anything can cure it. What offers the best chance of permanent cure?
opts: Wide excision of the affected areas
Correct. Chances of permanent cure are best with wide excision of the affected areas. Large fluctuant cysts are incised and drained, but that manages an episode rather than curing the disease.
Long-term systemic antibiotics
Some advocate long-term systemic antibiotics, but the long-term outcomes are described as often poor. They control rather than cure.
Topical clindamycin used indefinitely
Mild topical steroid creams combined with topical antibiotics are favoured for mild disease, but they do not eliminate the affected apocrine-bearing tissue.
Intralesional triamcinolone acetonide injections
Intralesional triamcinolone decreases the size of draining sinuses, which is a useful symptomatic measure rather than a definitive one.
Incision and drainage of each cyst as it develops
Incision and drainage relieves individual large fluctuant cysts. Because the disease recurs in the same apocrine regions, repeated drainage never becomes a cure.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 79

C.io: 7 — Recall counseling strategies to help patients adhere to treatment plans
C.q: A 61-year-old woman has not been taking a medication prescribed for her three months ago and is reluctant to say why. Which barriers to treatment and medication adherence should be considered?
opts: Patient motivation only
Framing non-adherence as a motivational failing overlooks the structural and educational barriers explicitly listed.
Cost of medications only
Cost is one barrier among several, and addressing it alone leaves understanding and cultural factors unaddressed.
Cost, health literacy, and cultural or religious factors

Correct. Barriers to treatment and medication adherence include the cost and affordability of medications or services, low health literacy or lack of understanding, and cultural or religious considerations.
Barriers cannot be anticipated
The named barriers are precisely those a clinician can anticipate and address during counselling.
Dosing complexity only
Regimen complexity is a real-world issue but is not among the barriers named here.
C.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 29

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 26-year-old woman presents with painful grouped vesicles on an erythematous base. The clinician performs a bedside Tzanck smear, which shows cytologic changes consistent with a herpesvirus. What is the most appropriate next step?
opts: Bacterial culture and sensitivity

Bacterial culture and sensitivity identifies bacteria and determines appropriate antibiotic therapy. The cytology has already pointed to a virus, so a bacterial culture answers a question that is no longer being asked.
Direct immunofluorescence of perilesional skin

Direct immunofluorescence detects abnormal immune deposits such as antibodies or complement in skin tissue and is used for autoimmune blistering disease. It is not the confirmatory test for a viral vesicular eruption.
Accept the Tzanck smear as definitive

A Tzanck smear shows herpesvirus cytologic changes but cannot distinguish herpes simplex virus from varicella zoster virus. Treating it as definitive attributes more specificity to the test than it has.
A potassium hydroxide preparation
A potassium hydroxide preparation detects fungal elements. It has no role in confirming a viral cytologic finding.
Confirm with viral polymerase chain reaction

Correct. A Tzanck smear provides rapid evaluation of vesicular lesions for herpesvirus cytologic changes, but polymerase chain reaction is preferred for confirmation. Viral polymerase chain reaction detects the genetic material of the virus and identifies which herpesvirus is responsible.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 32

C.io: b — Discuss unique considerations of methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus skin infections, including risk factors, presentation, and treatment
C.q: A 7-year-old boy and his mother, who teaches at his school, both present with honey-crusted perioral lesions. In which patient with impetigo should a culture be obtained rather than relying on clinical appearance alone?
opts: Any patient on topical mupirocin
Mupirocin is adequate for most cases of limited non-bullous impetigo and as effective as oral therapy. Its use does not itself indicate culture.
Any child under five
Impetigo is common in infants and children and is most often diagnosed by clinical appearance. Age alone does not create the resistance risk that prompts culture.
Only those who failed oral antibiotics
Waiting for treatment failure delays identification in exactly the high-risk groups where resistance is anticipated in advance.
A healthcare worker or teacher

Correct. Cultures are obtained if the patient is at high risk for methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus infection, with healthcare workers and teachers given as the examples, or if acute post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis is a concern.
Any patient with honey-coloured crusting
Honey-coloured adherent crust is the classic appearance of non-bullous impetigo and is what allows a clinical diagnosis. It is a reason not to culture rather than a reason to.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 93

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 9-year-old presents with a fever above 39.5 degrees Celsius for three days, headache, and now a rash that began on the ankles and wrists and is spreading centrally. What is the treatment, and does his age change it?
opts: Supportive care only

The disease is life threatening if not treated, with severe cardiac, gastrointestinal, hepatic, neurological, ophthalmological, renal, and pulmonary manifestations following delayed or inadequate treatment.
Withhold until serology returns
The indirect immunofluorescence assay is the gold standard test, but waiting for it costs the time in which treatment determines survival.
Amoxicillin; doxycycline is contraindicated

The usual paediatric caution about tetracyclines does not override treatment here — doxycycline dosing for children is specified, and delayed or inadequate treatment leads to severe and life-threatening complications.
Intravenous ceftriaxone for 14 days
Ceftriaxone is used intravenously for certain manifestations of Lyme disease rather than for rickettsial infection.
Doxycycline, used in children for this infection

Correct. Rocky Mountain spotted fever is treated with doxycycline in adults at 100 mg every 12 hours for 5 to 10 days, the same in pregnant women, and in children at 2.2 mg per kilogram every 12 hours. The illness is life threatening if untreated.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 86

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 48-year-old woman with papulopustular rosacea has Demodex-associated disease that has not responded to topical metronidazole. What topical agent is described as superior for this situation?
opts: A high-potency topical corticosteroid
Facial corticosteroids drive perioral dermatitis and can worsen rosacea, and they are not part of its management.
Metronidazole 0.75 to 1 percent gel at a higher frequency

Metronidazole is the first-line topical for papulopustular disease, and it has already failed here. Increasing the frequency of an agent described as inferior for Demodex-associated disease does not address the reason it failed.
Azelaic acid 15 to 20 percent

Azelaic acid is effective for both papulopustular and erythematotelangiectatic rosacea through anti-inflammatory and anti-keratinising effects, so it is a legitimate option. But it is not the agent singled out for Demodex-associated disease.
Brimonidine gel
Brimonidine is a topical vasoconstrictor aimed at the erythema of rosacea rather than at the inflammatory papules and pustules or the mite burden.
Ivermectin 1 percent cream

Correct. Ivermectin 1 percent cream is described as superior to metronidazole for Demodex-associated papulopustular rosacea, reflecting the contribution of Demodex folliculorum mite overgrowth to the pathogenesis.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 69

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 2-week-old neonate develops blisters at sites of handling and diapering, and genetic testing is planned. Which subtype carries the greatest long-term risk of squamous cell carcinoma and requires the most intensive multidisciplinary surveillance?
opts: Kindler syndrome
Kindler syndrome is a recognised form within the classification but is not the subtype singled out for scarring and squamous cell carcinoma surveillance in this lecture.
Epidermolysis bullosa simplex

Simplex disease results from keratin 5 and 14 mutations with intraepidermal cleavage, is localised to the palms and soles, and heals without scarring. Absence of scarring is why it does not carry the same malignancy burden.
Acquired epidermolysis bullosa
Epidermolysis bullosa acquisita is an autoimmune rather than inherited disease and falls outside the four inherited types classified by cleavage level.
Junctional epidermolysis bullosa

Junctional disease is generalised with poor wound healing, nail dystrophy, and enamel defects, and it is severe. But the scarring that drives squamous cell carcinoma surveillance characterises the dystrophic form.
Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa

Correct. Dystrophic epidermolysis bullosa causes severe scarring, and the multidisciplinary team includes haematology and oncology specifically for squamous cell carcinoma surveillance. Scarring subtypes carry the malignancy risk.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 30

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 55-year-old man with diabetes has an asymptomatic brownish patch in a skin fold noted on routine examination. Where is erythrasma most commonly found, and what is the typical symptom profile?
opts: Inner thighs, groin, and fourth toe web; often silent

Correct. The most common sites are the inner thighs, crural region, scrotum, and between the fourth and fifth toes, with the axilla, under the breasts, and intergluteal folds less common. It is usually asymptomatic and may be pruritic.
Around the nose and mouth, honey-crusted
Perioral honey-coloured crusting is non-bullous impetigo, a superficial epidermal infection of children.
Scalp, thighs, and trunk, with follicular pustules
Those are the common sites of folliculitis, whose lesions are pustules pierced by a central hair.
Axilla, groin, and perineum, recurrent and painful
That distribution and symptom profile belong to hidradenitis suppurativa, which affects apocrine-bearing skin with recurrence more than twice in six months.
Face and lower leg, with sudden high fever
The face and lower extremity with sudden high fever describes erysipelas, an acute streptococcal infection rather than a chronic asymptomatic intertriginous one.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 81

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 57-year-old man has confirmed toxic epidermal necrolysis with epidermal detachment of 45 percent of his body surface area. What is the mandatory disposition?
opts: Outpatient management
Outpatient management of a condition with epidermal detachment exceeding 30 percent of the body surface area and mortality up to 35 percent is not tenable at any level of follow-up.
Emergency department observation
The eruption progresses over days, so waiting for stabilisation in an emergency department delays the resuscitative and wound care that determine survival.
A general medical ward

A general ward cannot provide the fluid resuscitation, wound care, and temperature and infection control this condition demands. With mortality up to 30 to 35 percent, the level of care is not discretionary.
A burn unit or intensive care unit

Correct. Burn unit or intensive care admission is mandatory for all cases of toxic epidermal necrolysis, together with immediate discontinuation of all suspect drugs, fluid resuscitation estimated as for major burns, and non-adhesive biological dressings.
A surgical ward for debridement
Wound care uses non-adhesive biological dressings such as biobrane or porcine xenograft. Aggressive surgical debridement is not the described approach.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 90

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 16-year-old girl has multiple 1 to 2 mm firm skin-coloured papules symmetrically distributed on the lower eyelids that appeared around puberty. What is the origin of these lesions?
opts: Benign neoplasms of apocrine glands
Apocrine gland inflammation characterises hidradenitis suppurativa. Syringomas arise from the eccrine duct.
Proliferation of dermal capillaries
Capillary proliferation produces cherry angiomas, which are red and blanch with pressure.
Benign neoplasms of eccrine ducts
Correct. Syringomas are benign neoplasms of eccrine sweat ducts. They appear at puberty and are more common in females, presenting as multiple 1 to 2 mm papules and usually asymptomatic.
Collections of lipid-laden macrophages

Lipid-laden macrophages form xanthelasma, which appears as soft yellow cholesterol plaques and is on the syringoma differential — but xanthelasma is yellow and plaque-like rather than small firm papules.
Hyperplasia of sebaceous glands around a central pore
Sebaceous hyperplasia produces whitish-yellow or skin-coloured papules with a central dell, typically in older adults rather than at puberty.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 58

C.io: 4 — Discuss clinical principles and decision-making
C.q: A clinician has settled quickly on a diagnosis for a 50-year-old man and is now gathering data that would support it. Which suggestion for good decision-making addresses confirmation bias most directly?
opts: Defer decisions until all results return
Deferring indefinitely is not among the suggestions and can be harmful in an unstable patient.
Apply a guideline rule early
Guidelines are usually straightforward and easy to use but should be applied appropriately, and reaching for one early does not counteract a bias toward one's initial impression.
Ask questions that would disprove your diagnosis

Correct. Among the suggestions for good decision-making is to ask questions to disprove rather than confirm, alongside slowing down, being aware of base rates, considering what data is truly relevant, and actively seeking alternative diagnoses.
Rely on quick pattern recognition
The intuitive system works in straightforward or common situations but is the mode in which confirmation bias operates most freely, which is why slowing down is advised.
Gather all data regardless of relevance
The advice is to consider what data is truly relevant. Indiscriminate data gathering produces incidental findings without improving reasoning.
C.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 26

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 52-year-old woman of Mediterranean descent presents with painful mouth erosions that began three months ago, followed by skin lesions. Examination shows flaccid bullae and widespread crusted erosions on the scalp, chest, axillae, and groin that bleed easily and are painful. Lateral pressure on normal-appearing skin causes the superficial layers to slip away. What does the biopsy most likely demonstrate?
opts: Band-like lymphocytes in the dermis
A band-like lymphocytic infiltrate is the histological signature of lichen planus, which presents with pruritic purple polygonal papules rather than a blistering disorder with mucosal onset.
Subepithelial blistering, no acantholysis

This is the bullous pemphigoid pattern, and the comparison table pairs it with tense firm blisters and a negative Nikolsky's sign. This patient has flaccid bullae and a positive Nikolsky's sign, which is the opposite half of that table.
Acantholysis with intraepithelial blisters

Correct. Pemphigus is characterised by loss of keratinocyte-to-keratinocyte adhesion, termed acantholysis, producing intraepithelial blisters. The oral onset, flaccid easily ruptured bullae, and positive Nikolsky's sign all identify pemphigus, and biopsy demonstrating acantholysis is the diagnostic finding.
Neutrophils in a row at the junction

That light-microscopy description belongs to bullous pemphigoid. It is a real finding but attached to the wrong disease for a patient with oral-onset flaccid bullae and epidermal slippage on pressure.
Granular immunoglobulin A at papillary tips

Granular immunoglobulin A at the papillary tips is the direct immunofluorescence finding of dermatitis herpetiformis, which presents with grouped pruritic vesicles on extensor surfaces rather than painful oral erosions and flaccid bullae.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 132

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 30-year-old woman with tinea corporis asks whether the infection can spread to her mouth, and a student asks why dermatophytes never involve mucous membranes. What is the correct explanation?
opts: They require sebum
Sebum matters in tinea capitis, where post-pubertal changes in sebum fatty acid content are believed to inhibit dermatophyte growth. But the organisms depend on keratin rather than requiring sebum.
Salivary enzymes kill them
The limitation is the absence of dead keratin rather than an antimicrobial property of saliva. Candida, which is not a dermatophyte, colonises mucosa freely.
They can involve mucosa if immunocompromised
The constraint is structural rather than immunological. Immunosuppression extends the severity and extent of dermatophytosis but does not create keratin where there is none.
They are obligate intracellular organisms
Dermatophytes are not intracellular organisms. They live within keratinised tissue rather than inside cells.
They survive only on dead keratin
Correct. Dermatophytes infect and survive only on dead keratin, involving the superficial portion of the skin at the stratum corneum, plus hair and nails. They cannot survive on mucous membranes.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 6

C.io: b — Identify medical care strategies for pigmented skin lesions in adult and elderly populations
C.q: A 32-year-old fair-skinned woman has numerous moles under 6 mm with homogeneous surface and colour. One lesion is very dark brown to black. What is the significance of that lesion?
opts: It is suspicious and warrants evaluation

Correct. Common acquired melanocytic naevi are usually less than 6 mm with homogeneous surface and colour, round to oval with sharp demarcation. A very dark brown or black lesion on a light-skinned individual is specifically flagged as suspicious.
It confirms melanoma without biopsy
Suspicion warrants evaluation and biopsy rather than a diagnosis made on colour alone.
It is expected with many moles; no action

Increased numbers of moles do raise melanoma risk, which makes this superficially reassuring reasoning. But a single lesion diverging in colour from its neighbours is the specific finding singled out as suspicious.
It is a Spitz nevus; always benign
Spitz naevi are solitary, pink or red, hairless, firm, and dome-shaped, usually benign but sometimes resembling melanoma. They are not dark brown or black.
It is a blue nevus; no evaluation
Blue naevi are blue, blue-grey, or blue-black and occur at characteristic sites including the dorsal hands and feet, scalp, and sacral region, and larger lesions are biopsied.
C.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 36

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 21-year-old man presents with sudden pain and swelling over the sacrum in the gluteal cleft. Examination shows a warm, tender, erythematous fluctuant mass with purulent drainage. What is the appropriate management of this acute presentation?
opts: Magnetic resonance imaging before any intervention
No diagnostic testing is usually needed. Imaging would delay the drainage that relieves the abscess.
Incision and drainage

Correct. An acute pilonidal abscess requires incision and drainage. The condition arises when a dimple over the coccyx draws in hair and debris leading to follicular plugging, and ingrown hairs prevent drainage and promote abscess formation.
Warm compresses and observation
Observation of a fluctuant, draining abscess allows it to enlarge and extend rather than resolve.
Immediate wide surgical excision of the natal cleft
Definitive excision addresses chronic disease with sinus tracts. It is not the management of an acute abscess presentation.
Oral antibiotics alone
An antibiotic will not evacuate a fluctuant collection, and fluctuance is specifically the palpation finding indicating fluid. Drainage is required.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 43

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 64-year-old man has a biopsy-proven keratoacanthoma on the dorsal forearm. What is the standard of care, and what margin is used for elliptical excision?
opts: Observation alone
Regression does occur after 3 to 6 months, but the lesion may continue growing or rarely metastasise, and it cannot be distinguished from squamous cell carcinoma without histology.
Excision with 5 mm margins

Correct. The standard of care is to excise or destroy the tumour, preferred because of possible malignancy, with elliptical excision using 5 mm margins. Mohs surgery may be indicated for large or recurrent lesions or those in cosmetically sensitive locations.
Excision with 1 mm margins
A 1 mm margin is inadequate for a lesion excised specifically because of possible malignancy.
Intralesional corticosteroid
Intralesional steroids are used for keloids and hypertrophic scars, and for inflamed epidermoid cysts. They are not the treatment for a possible keratinocytic malignancy.
Cryotherapy without histology
Destroying the lesion without histology forfeits the diagnosis, which matters given the squamous cell carcinoma differential.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 52

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
C.q: A 76-year-old man has a biopsy-proven invasive cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma on the dorsal forearm. What is the preferred management?
opts: Topical imiquimod or fluorouracil
Imiquimod, topical fluorouracil, or curettage and electrodesiccation are options for carcinoma in situ without high-risk features. Applying them to invasive disease under-treats it.
Surgical excision or Mohs micrographic surgery

Correct. Surgical excision or Mohs micrographic surgery is preferred for invasive squamous cell carcinoma, with at least annual skin and lymph node examination and closer intervals for high-risk or immunosuppressed patients. All suspected invasive lesions are referred to dermatology or an experienced surgeon.
Radiotherapy
Surgery is the preferred modality. Radiotherapy has a role in selected patients rather than as universal first line.
Cryotherapy
Cryotherapy is a lesion-directed therapy for actinic keratosis. It is not the treatment for invasive carcinoma, and follow-up is required in any case.
Observation alone
Squamous cell carcinoma carries genuine metastatic potential, which is why lymph node examination is part of follow-up.
C.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 26

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: Computed tomography of a 48-year-old man with suspected necrotizing fasciitis shows gas in the soft tissue fascial planes. What does this indicate about the likely organism?
opts: Gas suggests Clostridium, not group A streptococcus
Correct. Gas may be present with Clostridium perfringens infection but is not present with group A streptococcal infection. Ultrasound is also useful for demonstrating air bubbles in soft tissue.
Gas is present in every case
Absence of gas does not exclude necrotizing fasciitis, and group A streptococcal disease specifically does not produce it. Requiring gas for the diagnosis would miss the common streptococcal form.
Gas suggests group A streptococcus, not Clostridium
The two organisms are reversed. A clinician using this rule would exclude clostridial infection on the very finding that suggests it.
Gas means the infection is superficial
Gas in the fascial planes indicates deep involvement. Necrotizing fasciitis involves the tissue surrounding muscles, nerves, fat, and blood vessels.
Gas means a fungal cause
Necrotizing fasciitis is a bacterial infection that may be polymicrobial with aerobic, anaerobic, or mixed flora. Gas points to a gas-forming bacterium rather than a fungus.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 129

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pigmented skin lesions
C.q: A 19-year-old woman has a blue-grey papule under 1 cm on the dorsum of the hand. What are blue naevi composed of, and how does management differ by lesion size?
opts: Keratinocytes; cryotherapy
Keratinocytic proliferation describes seborrheic keratosis. Blue naevi are melanocytic.
Dermal melanocytes; biopsy larger lesions

Correct. Blue naevi are composed of deeply pigmented spindle or epithelioid melanocytes in the dermis. Diagnosis is clinical for small lesions and by biopsy for larger ones, with observation and biopsy or excision if changes are noted.
Epidermal melanocytes; always clinical
The melanocytes lie in the dermis, which is what gives the lesion its blue colour, and larger lesions require biopsy rather than clinical diagnosis alone.
Lipid-laden macrophages; lipid screening
Lipid-laden macrophages form xanthelasma, which warrants hyperlipidaemia screening.
Dilated capillaries; blanches
Dilated dermal vessels produce vascular lesions that blanch. Blue naevi are pigmented and do not blanch.
C.cite: CMS I Pigmented Skin Lesions - Shahsv-2.pptx, Slide 40

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 19-year-old woman is to begin oral isotretinoin for recalcitrant nodular acne. What safety requirements apply?
opts: Monthly liver tests, no pregnancy testing
Laboratory monitoring accompanies isotretinoin, but omitting pregnancy testing removes the single most important safeguard for a potent teratogen in a woman of childbearing age.
Pregnancy tests before, monthly, and 5 weeks after

Correct. Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen. Negative pregnancy tests are mandatory prior to initiation, monthly, and 5 weeks post treatment, only one month is dispensed at a time, and providers must be registered.
No specific requirements
Monotherapy describes how the drug is combined with others, not how it is monitored. Isotretinoin carries the strictest prescribing requirements of any acne agent.
Pregnancy tests before and one week after
The post-treatment interval is wrong. Testing is required 5 weeks after treatment, and shortening it to a week would clear a patient while the drug's teratogenic risk persists.
A pregnancy test before starting only
A single baseline test leaves the entire treatment course and the washout period unmonitored, which is exactly the window the monthly and post-treatment testing exists to cover.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 30

C.io: b — Identify medical strategies for common benign skin lesions in infants, adolescents, adults and the elderly
C.q: A 6-year-old boy has eight light brown macules greater than 5 mm and freckling in both axillae. What condition does this suggest, and what is the freckling called?
opts: Neurofibromatosis type 1; Darier sign
The condition is right but the sign is wrong. Darier sign is urtication of a lesion after stroking and indicates mastocytosis.
Neurofibromatosis type 2

Neurofibromatosis type 2 involves the NF2 gene on chromosome 22, but the cutaneous manifestations described — café au lait spots, cutaneous neurofibromas, intertriginous freckling, and plexiform neurofibromas — belong to type 1, whose gene is on chromosome 17.
Postinflammatory hyperpigmentation
Post-inflammatory change requires prior inflammation at the site, and it would not produce discrete café au lait macules elsewhere on the body.
Multiple lentigines from sun exposure
Crowe's sign freckles do become more prominent with sun exposure, but they occur in intertriginous sites that are largely sun-protected, which is what makes them notable.
Neurofibromatosis type 1; Crowe's sign

Correct. Café au lait spots are often the first manifestation of neurofibromatosis type 1, defined as light tan to brown macules over 5 mm prepubertally. Intertriginous freckling in the axillary and inguinal regions is Crowe's sign, with freckles smaller than 5 mm.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 102

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 26-year-old woman has grouped papules and papulopustules around the mouth, and the clinician is distinguishing perioral dermatitis from its principal differential diagnoses. What finding would most specifically point to acne vulgaris instead?
opts: Open or closed comedones
Correct. Acne vulgaris is more likely when open or closed comedones are present. Perioral dermatitis produces grouped monomorphic papules, papulovesicles, or papulopustules without comedones.
Central erythema with telangiectasia
Central facial erythema, flushing, telangiectasia, papulopustules, or ocular symptoms describe rosacea, which is a different item on the differential.
Papulopustules on the face
Papulopustules occur in perioral dermatitis, rosacea, and acne alike. A finding common to all three differentials cannot select among them.
Sparing beside the vermilion border
That sparing is characteristic of perioral dermatitis itself, so it argues for the diagnosis rather than for acne.
Scale on scalp and nasolabial folds
Prominent scale at those sites describes seborrheic dermatitis, the third differential listed, rather than acne.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 100

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 70-year-old man has a painful vesicular eruption in a band across one side of the chest. What is the single most characteristic distributional feature of herpes zoster?
opts: It follows a Christmas tree pattern
The Christmas tree pattern following cleavage lines describes pityriasis rosea, which follows a herald patch.
It crosses the midline symmetrically
This is the direct inversion of the defining feature. A bilateral symmetric eruption should prompt a different diagnosis entirely.
It is generalised over trunk and face
That distribution describes primary varicella rather than reactivation, and varicella shows multiple stages simultaneously.
It stops abruptly at the midline

Correct. Blisters are confined to the cutaneous distribution of one or two adjacent sensory nerves and abruptly stop at the midline. Thoracic dermatomes are most frequently involved at about 55 percent, followed by cranial at about 20 percent.
It is confined to skin folds
Flexural and intertriginous distribution suggests candidal intertrigo, erythrasma, or inverse psoriasis rather than a dermatomal viral reactivation.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 100

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 48-year-old man has soft yellow plaques on the medial aspects of both upper eyelids. What do they contain, and what should be done?
opts: Lipid-laden macrophages; screen for hyperlipidaemia

Correct. Xanthelasma consists of soft yellow cholesterol plaques formed by collections of lipid-laden macrophages. They are associated with lipid disorders, so screening for hyperlipidaemia is indicated, and they may signify increased cardiac risk.
Eccrine duct neoplasms of puberty
Syringomas are eccrine duct neoplasms of the lower eyelids appearing at puberty, and they are firm skin-coloured papules rather than soft yellow plaques.
Lipid-laden macrophages; no investigation needed
The composition is right but stopping at cosmesis discards the reason the lesion matters. The association with lipid disorders and increased cardiac risk is exactly what makes screening worthwhile.
Keratin in an epithelial cyst; excise
Keratin within enclosed epithelium describes an epidermoid cyst, which is a firm moveable nodule with a central punctum rather than a soft yellow eyelid plaque.
Dilated capillaries; laser therapy
Dilated capillaries produce telangiectasias, which are blanchable and vascular rather than yellow and lipid laden.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 104

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological infestations
C.q: A 41-year-old woman has recurrent grouped bites appearing each morning after sleeping in her own bed. What is essential in the management of a bedbug infestation beyond treating the patient's skin?
opts: A professional exterminator

Correct. Management of the patient is symptomatic with local wound care, topical antiseptic or antibiotic cream for secondary infection, and topical corticosteroids or oral antihistamines for pruritus. A professional exterminator is necessary to eradicate the infestation itself.
Washing bedding at 60 degrees Celsius alone
High-heat laundering at 60 degrees Celsius is the environmental measure specified for scabies mites. Bedbugs live in cracks and crevices of furniture and walls, which laundering does not reach.
A pediculicide to the skin
Pediculicides treat lice living on the host. Bedbugs feed and then return to the environment.
No environmental action
Without eradication the bites simply continue, which is why professional extermination is described as necessary.
Treating all contacts with permethrin
Contact treatment applies to scabies, where household members are treated. Bedbugs are not carried on the person in the same way.
C.cite: CMS I Dermatological Infestations - Shahsv.pptx, Slide 35

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
C.q: A 52-year-old man is diagnosed with a melanoma on the upper back that had spread radially for months before entering a vertical growth phase. What is the most common subtype of melanoma?
opts: Superficial spreading melanoma
Correct. Superficial spreading melanoma accounts for about two-thirds of cases, arises on intermittently sun-exposed skin, and evolves radially before entering vertical growth.
Nodular melanoma
Nodular melanoma is a recognised major subtype characterised by early vertical growth, but it is not the commonest.
Lentigo maligna melanoma
Lentigo maligna arises on chronically sun-exposed skin of older adults with a slow radial growth phase, but it is not the most common subtype.
Acral lentiginous melanoma
Acral lentiginous melanoma is one of the four major subtypes and is important because it occurs on palms, soles, and nail units in any skin tone, but it is uncommon overall.
Amelanotic melanoma
Amelanotic melanoma is a presentation that lacks pigment and appears on several differentials. It is not a majority subtype.
C.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 41

C.io: 4 — Discuss clinical principles and decision-making
C.q: A student uses the VINDICATE mnemonic to build a differential for a 72-year-old man brought to the emergency department with confusion. What do the letters stand for?
opts: Vascular, infectious, neoplastic, degenerative, iatrogenic, congenital, autoimmune, trauma, endocrine

Correct. VINDICATE is a category-based framework: vascular, infectious, neoplastic, degenerative, iatrogenic, congenital, autoimmune, trauma, and endocrine or metabolic. Applied to confusion it yields stroke, meningitis, brain tumour, Alzheimer disease, and so on.
Vascular, inflammatory, neurological, drug-related, idiopathic, cardiac, allergic, toxic, environmental
Several of these categories are plausible in isolation but they are not the letters of this mnemonic, and a misremembered framework produces a differential with systematic gaps.
A physical examination sequence
VINDICATE is a differential diagnosis framework organised by disease category rather than an examination sequence.
A checklist for appraising evidence
Evaluating the quality and validity of evidence is a step in evidence-based practice, separate from this mnemonic.
A pretest probability score
The mnemonic generates categories to consider rather than producing a numerical probability.
C.cite: 1. svClinical Reasoning and Problem Solving.pptx, Slide 16

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 43-year-old factory worker splashes a concentrated alkali solution on the forearm, while a colleague of the same age has had weeks of soreness from repeated soap exposure. How does the timing of an irritant reaction to a strong alkali differ from that of a reaction to a mild irritant such as soap?
opts: Alkalis over weeks; soaps in minutes
The two are reversed. Assigning the slow course to the corrosive agent is the error most likely to lead to an untreated chemical injury.
Both act only after weeks
This would delay recognition of a chemical burn. Strong alkalis can produce symptoms within minutes and can cause necrosis, so treating the exposure as a slow cumulative process is dangerous.
Alkalis act in minutes to a day; soaps over weeks

Correct. Symptoms present differently depending on the exposure: mild irritants such as soaps may present with subacute symptoms that progress over weeks, while alkalis and acids may present minutes after exposure or delayed up to 24 hours or more. Concentrated agents can lead to chemical burns and necrosis.
Neither acts before 48 to 72 hours
A delayed hypersensitivity time course belongs to allergic contact dermatitis, which is a type IV reaction. Irritant dermatitis is direct barrier damage rather than immunological sensitisation.
Alkalis act systemically; soaps locally
Both are local reactions at the site of contact. Concentrated agents can cause deeper local injury including chemical burns and necrosis, but the reaction remains cutaneous.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 81

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: A 45-year-old man has a small area of cellulitis of the forearm with minimal pain, no systemic signs, and no comorbidity. In which patient with cellulitis is no diagnostic workup required?
opts: Limited area, minimal pain, no systemic signs

Correct. Cellulitis is usually a clinical diagnosis, and no workup is needed when there is a limited area of involvement, minimal pain, no systemic signs, and no risk factor for serious illness such as extremes of age or immunocompromise.
Any cellulitis of the lower leg
The lower leg is the most common site, so this describes the majority of cases rather than a low-risk subset. Site does not determine whether investigation is needed.
Only patients under 40
Extremes of age are one risk factor among several, and a single age cut-off does not capture immunocompromise, extent, or systemic signs.
Any patient who is afebrile
Fever may be absent depending on severity, so a normal temperature alone does not establish that the patient is low risk. Extent, pain, and comorbidity all contribute.
Any patient already on antibiotics
Current antibiotic use does not remove the need for assessment, and failure to respond within 48 hours should raise necrotizing fasciitis.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 109

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 44-year-old fair-skinned woman newly diagnosed with rosacea asks which trigger is most important to control. What is the most accurate answer?
opts: Alcohol, described as the most universal trigger

Alcohol is a genuine and commonly reported trigger, which makes this the closest wrong answer, but sun exposure is the one identified as most universal. Focusing counselling on alcohol alone would leave the dominant exposure unaddressed.
Dairy products, which drive Demodex overgrowth
Demodex folliculorum overgrowth contributes to the pathogenesis, but dairy is not a listed trigger and does not drive the mite burden.
Topical corticosteroid use, which is the primary cause
Topical corticosteroid exposure is the most important modifiable association of perioral dermatitis rather than of rosacea, and steroids can worsen rosacea rather than cause it.
Sun exposure, described as the most universal trigger
Correct. Sun exposure is named as the most universal trigger of rosacea, alongside heat, alcohol, spicy foods, and stress. Chronic ultraviolet exposure is also a listed risk factor.
Cold weather, which is the dominant environmental trigger
Heat rather than cold appears among the common triggers. Advising avoidance of cold would misdirect the patient's efforts.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 67

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, referrals, patient education and prognosis of cutaneous bacterial infections
C.q: Four women in their twenties present on the same clinic list with acne of differing severity and history. For which patient is a combined oral contraceptive most appropriate as acne therapy?
opts: A man with papulopustular acne
Combined oral contraceptives are not applicable to male patients, whose moderate disease is treated with a topical retinoid, an oral antibiotic, and benzoyl peroxide.
Mild comedonal acne, never treated
Mild comedonal acne is treated first with a topical retinoid. Starting systemic hormonal therapy before any topical trial reverses the treatment ladder.
A woman planning pregnancy soon
A patient planning pregnancy is not an appropriate candidate for contraceptive-based therapy, and the treatment goal and the reproductive goal are in direct conflict.
Hyperandrogenism, unresponsive to topical therapy

Correct. Oral contraceptives are considered for patients with hyperandrogenism and when acne is unresponsive to both topical retinoids and topical or oral antibiotics. Oestrogen decreases sebum production and reduces ovarian androgen production.
Any adolescent, as first-line therapy
Combined oral contraceptives sit well down the systemic treatment list and are considered for specific indications rather than used as universal first-line therapy.
C.cite: 4.  Cutaneous Bacterial Infections.pptx, Slide 28

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 29-year-old fair-skinned woman asks how to use sunscreen correctly before a beach holiday. What advice matches the guidance given?
opts: Only for Fitzpatrick types I to III

All Fitzpatrick types are susceptible to cumulative ultraviolet damage, photoaging, and skin cancer, though absolute risk varies. Restricting advice to fair skin types leaves darker-skinned patients uncounselled.
Broad-spectrum factor 30 daily, reapplied every 2 hours
Correct. Broad-spectrum sun protection factor 30 or above is advised for daily use and 50 or above for prolonged outdoor exposure, applied 15 minutes before sun exposure and reapplied every 2 hours.
Broad-spectrum factor 30 daily, applied once
The product choice is right but a single morning application is the commonest real-world failure. Reapplication every 2 hours is what maintains the protection the number implies.
Factor 15, reapplied only after swimming
Sun protection factor 15 falls below the recommended minimum of 30 for daily use, and restricting reapplication to after swimming leaves long dry exposures unprotected.
Physical barriers alone
Physical barriers are recommended alongside sunscreen rather than instead of it. Discarding sunscreen removes one of the two components of photoprotection.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 123

C.io: c — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 55-year-old man presents with a single intensely itchy patch on the posterior neck that has been present for over a year. He describes rubbing it frequently, particularly when stressed or trying to fall asleep. Examination shows a well-demarcated thickened plaque with exaggerated skin markings, excoriation, scale, and altered pigmentation. What is the central principle of management?
opts: Reassurance alone

Recurrence is expected unless the initiating itch is controlled, and telling a patient simply to stop scratching without addressing sleep, anxiety, neuropathic symptoms, and the primary dermatosis rarely succeeds.
Break the itch-scratch cycle

Correct. Lichen simplex chronicus results from repeated rubbing and scratching, so management centres on breaking the itch-scratch cycle with education, treatment of the trigger, emollients, behavioural substitution, nail care, and safe physical occlusion, alongside a limited course of an appropriate potent topical corticosteroid.
Surgical excision of the plaque

Excision treats the visible result while leaving the itch and the behaviour intact, so the plaque simply reforms. Biopsy is reserved for atypical, unilateral, nodular, ulcerated, or treatment-resistant plaques to exclude neoplasia.
Indefinite potent topical corticosteroid

A potent topical corticosteroid is used, but for a limited course. Continuing it indefinitely invites atrophy, striae, and telangiectasia, and it leaves the scratching behaviour that drives the plaque entirely unaddressed.
An oral antifungal
The thickening here is lichenification from chronic rubbing, not a fungal infection. Treating it as tinea leaves the true driver untouched and delays effective management.
C.cite: 2. General Dermatology I.pptx, Slide 183

C.io: 1 — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of pre-malignant and malignant cutaneous lesions
C.q: A 78-year-old fair-skinned farmer has a small red, conical, hard nodule on the pinna that has ulcerated and grown over two months. What is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Basal cell carcinoma

Basal cell carcinoma is the most common form of cancer and is driven by intense intermittent exposure, but its nodular form is a pearly translucent papule with telangiectasias rather than a hard conical ulcerating nodule.
Actinic keratosis
Actinic keratoses are small sandpapery papules 0.2 to 0.6 cm. Rapid growth, ulceration, and a hard nodule are the red flags that mark progression beyond that stage.
Amelanotic melanoma
Amelanotic melanoma is on the differential, but the classic conical hard ulcerating nodule on chronically sun-exposed skin of an older fair-skinned outdoor worker fits keratinocyte carcinoma.
Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma

Correct. Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma is the second most common form of skin cancer, usually following prolonged cumulative sun exposure, and may arise from an actinic keratosis. The classic presentation is a small red conical hard nodule that may ulcerate, or a non-healing ulcer, warty nodule, or irregular pink plaque with haemorrhagic crust.
Keratoacanthoma
Keratoacanthoma is on the differential and can regress, which is exactly why biopsy is the only reliable way to distinguish it from squamous cell carcinoma.
C.cite: Premalignant and Malignant Cutaneous Lesions - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 22

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
C.q: A 63-year-old man has several soft whitish-yellow papules 3 to 5 mm on the forehead, each with a central dell. He is worried about skin cancer. What test can distinguish this from the main differential?
opts: Dermoscopy
Correct. Basal cell carcinoma is the principal differential for sebaceous hyperplasia, and dermoscopy can distinguish between them. Biopsy is performed if malignancy concern persists.
A Wood's lamp examination
A Wood lamp evaluates pigment changes in selected fungal and bacterial infections. It does not differentiate sebaceous hyperplasia from basal cell carcinoma.
Serum lipid measurement
Lipid screening is indicated for xanthelasma, which is associated with lipid disorders. Sebaceous hyperplasia reflects sebocyte turnover changes with age rather than a lipid disorder.
A potassium hydroxide preparation
A potassium hydroxide preparation detects fungal elements and has no role in distinguishing two non-infectious papular lesions.
No test; excise every lesion
Dermoscopy is available and non-invasive, and biopsy is reserved for continuing malignancy concern. Excising every lesion is unnecessary.
C.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 111

C.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
C.q: A 24-year-old man has tinea corporis, and the clinician wants an antifungal that works by destroying the fungal cell membrane rather than by blocking ergosterol synthesis. Which agent belongs to that class, and how is the class recognised by name?
opts: Terbinafine, an imidazole, recognisable by the ending -azole
Terbinafine is correctly chosen but wrongly classified. It is an allylamine, and the -azole ending identifies the imidazoles instead.
Nystatin, a polyene that treats both Candida and dermatophytes
Topical nystatin treats Candida only, which is precisely why topical azoles are preferred when a dermatophyte may also be present.
Ketoconazole, an imidazole, recognisable by the ending -fine
Ketoconazole is an imidazole, and imidazoles block ergosterol synthesis rather than destroying the membrane directly. The naming clue also belongs to the allylamines.
Griseofulvin, an allylamine favoured for Trichophyton infection
Griseofulvin is often favoured for Microsporum infection in tinea capitis, whereas terbinafine is generally favoured for Trichophyton. Griseofulvin is not an allylamine.
Terbinafine, an allylamine, recognisable by the ending -fine

Correct. The allylamine class works by destroying the cell membranes of fungi, preventing growth and ultimately killing them, and its members end in -fine: terbinafine and naftifine. Imidazoles instead block synthesis of ergosterol, a vital component of the fungal cell membrane.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 5

C.io: c — Identify medical care strategies for cutaneous viral and fungal infections for infant, child, adolescent, adult and elderly populations
C.q: A 58-year-old woman and her 62-year-old husband, who takes an immunosuppressant, both ask about shingles vaccination. Who should receive the recombinant zoster vaccine, and at what interval?
opts: Two doses in childhood
The two-dose varicella vaccine is what is given in childhood to prevent primary infection. Recombinant zoster vaccine is for adults to prevent reactivation.
A single dose from age 50
The vaccine is a two-dose series. A single dose leaves the schedule incomplete and the patient inadequately protected.
Two doses from age 50, or 19 if immunosuppressed

Correct. Two doses of recombinant zoster vaccine are given to immunocompetent adults aged 50 years and over, and two doses to adults aged 19 and over who are or will be immunodeficient or immunosuppressed, with a standard interval of 2 to 6 months.
Two doses from age 65 only
The age threshold for immunocompetent adults is 50 rather than 65, and restricting it to 65 would leave a fifteen-year band of eligible adults unvaccinated.
Two doses only after an episode of zoster
Prior zoster is not the eligibility criterion. Vaccination is recommended by age and by immune status.
C.cite: 6. Fungal and Viral Skin Infections - Jaquith.pptx, Slide 110

C.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
C.q: A 36-year-old woman with deeply pigmented skin asks whether she needs sun protection at all. What does the Fitzpatrick skin type classification predict, and how should it guide counselling?
opts: The likelihood of rosacea
Fitzpatrick types I to III are a risk factor for rosacea, so the scale is referenced there, but predicting rosacea is not what the classification is for.
Baseline ultraviolet sensitivity; all types need care

Correct. Fitzpatrick skin type predicts baseline ultraviolet sensitivity and guides photoprotection counselling. All types are susceptible to cumulative ultraviolet damage, photoaging, and skin cancer, though absolute risk varies.
The severity of an existing sunburn

Sunburn severity is graded by degree — first degree confined to the epidermis, second degree with blistering and partial dermal involvement. Fitzpatrick type describes baseline sensitivity before any exposure.
The required sun protection factor alone
Broad-spectrum sun protection factor 30 or above is advised for daily use across the board, and physical barriers are recommended alongside sunscreen rather than instead of it.
Baseline sensitivity; types V and VI need none

The first half is right, which is what makes this the closest wrong answer, but exempting darker skin types from counselling contradicts the statement that all types are susceptible. This is the assumption that leads to later diagnosis of skin cancer in darker-skinned patients.
C.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 122

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
D.q: A 19-year-old woman whose sister developed a large keloid after ear piercing asks how to avoid the same problem. What is described as the most important element in the management of keloids?
opts: Compression for one week after injury
Compression therapy is used with pressure maintained over an extended period rather than for a single week, and it is a treatment rather than the overarching principle.
Prevention, including avoiding ear piercing

Correct. Prevention is described as the most important treatment. High-risk patients should be advised to avoid cosmetic procedures such as ear piercing, and post-surgical education includes avoiding stretching of an immature scar and avoiding hot baths.
Routine biopsy of every lesion
Biopsy is performed only if there is clinical doubt, because it may itself induce new scarring.
Early excision of every lesion
Excision carries a 50 to 100 percent recurrence rate with lesions often larger than the original, so early surgery is not the cornerstone.
Intralesional steroid alone
Intralesional steroids eventually flatten lesions and reduce collagen production, and they may cause tissue atrophy. They are one modality among several rather than the most important element.
D.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 15

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis for benign skin lesions
D.q: A 30-year-old man has a raised, firm scar that developed within four weeks of a surgical incision. It remains within the original incision line and has flattened slightly over the past year. What management options apply?
opts: Systemic corticosteroids over six weeks
Steroid delivery for scars is intralesional rather than systemic, which concentrates the effect and avoids systemic exposure.
No treatment is ever appropriate
Hypertrophic scars remain stable and regress with time, which is genuinely reassuring, but treatment options exist for symptoms and appearance and need not be withheld.
Intralesional steroid, silicone sheeting, or laser

Correct. Hypertrophic scar management includes intralesional injection of corticosteroid or 5-fluorouracil, compression therapy and silicone sheeting, surgical excision, and pulsed dye laser, which reduces scar erythema by reducing neovascularisation.
Excision alone, which never recurs
It is worth noting that excision of a keloid carries a 50 to 100 percent recurrence rate; even for hypertrophic scars, excision is one option among several rather than a guaranteed cure.
Cryotherapy is always contraindicated
Cryotherapy with liquid nitrogen appears among keloid treatments, where it flattens lesions but can cause hypopigmentation. It is not universally contraindicated.
D.cite: 7. Benign Skin Lesions Prof Griffenkranz 8-25-2025-2.pptx, Slide 23

D.io: a — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of dermatological conditions
D.q: A 28-year-old woman has a single asymptomatic annular ring of flesh-coloured papules on the dorsum of the foot. What proportion of cases does this variant represent, and what is the expected course?
opts: About 50 percent; invariably recurs
Neither figure nor course matches. The condition is described as self-limiting rather than invariably recurrent.
About 75 percent; needs lifelong immunosuppression

Systemic therapy and phototherapy are reserved for generalised or treatment-resistant disease through a dermatology referral. Committing localised asymptomatic disease to systemic immunosuppression is far beyond what it needs.
About 75 percent; progresses to malignancy
The proportion is right, which makes this the closest wrong answer, but granuloma annulare is benign and self-limiting. An oncology referral is considered only if lymphoma is separately suspected.
About 75 percent; benign and self-limiting

Correct. The localised variant accounts for about 75 percent of cases, presenting as flesh-coloured to erythematous papules in an annular ring on the dorsal hands, feet, and ankles, and is asymptomatic. Granuloma annulare is a benign, self-limiting granulomatous dermatosis.
About 25 percent; benign and self-limiting
The course is right but the proportion is reversed — localised disease is the common form at about 75 percent, and the generalised or disseminated variant is the minority.
D.cite: 3. Dermatology  II.pptx, Slide 50

D.io: b — Compare and contrast the etiologies, epidemiology, risk factors, clinical manifestations, differential diagnosis, diagnostic testing, management, appropriate referrals, patient education, and prognosis of cutaneous viral and fungal infections
D.q: A 7-year-old boy has scaly patches on the scalp with areas of hair loss and visible black dots where hairs have fractured. A potassium hydroxide preparation confirms fungal elements. His mother asks whether a medicated cream will be enough. What is the correct response?
opts: Oral therapy; topicals miss the hair shaft
